The Labour Department announced today (the 10th) that Wah So Ice & Cafe (Prince Edward) provided false information to the department during its local open recruitment when applying to import foreign workers. The department has imposed administrative sanctions, including immediately terminating the company's application and refusing to process any applications submitted by the company for the following year.

Wah So Ice & Cafe (Prince Edward) has been administratively sanctioned by the Labour Department for providing false information during the local open recruitment period.

A spokesperson for the Labour Department stated that after investigation, it was confirmed that Wah So Ice & Cafe (Prince Edward) had provided false information during the local open recruitment for waiters, junior cooks, and dishwashers when applying to import foreign workers, thereby violating the regulations of the "Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme." Consequently, administrative sanctions have been imposed. The department has immediately terminated the company's submitted application for importing foreign workers and refused to process any applications submitted by the company under the Enhanced Scheme for the following year.

The department emphasised that employers importing foreign workers must strictly comply with the scheme's regulations, including prioritising the employment of suitable local workers. Should employers violate labour or immigration laws, the Enhanced Scheme, or the standard employment contract requirements, the Labour Department will impose administrative sanctions, including terminating applications already submitted by the employer, revoking any import worker approvals already granted to the employer, and refusing to process applications subsequently submitted by the employer.

According to Legislative Council data, since the launch of the Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme in September 2023, and up to March this year, the Labour Department has received a total of 1,048 complaints, completed investigation on 287 cases, and imposed administrative sanctions on 35 employers found to have violated the Employees' Compensation Ordinance, occupational safety and health legislation, the Immigration Ordinance, or the requirements of the Enhanced Scheme.
